records.sourceFile: Reasons for prescription opioid use while playing in the National Football League as risk factors for current use and misuse among former players.pdf

paper.citation: Dunne EM, Striley CW, Mannes ZL, Asken BM, Ennis N, Cottler LB. Reasons for prescription opioid use while playing in the National Football League as risk factors for current use and misuse among former players. Clin J Sport Med. 2020;30(6):544-549.
paper.abstract: This secondary analysis examined whether the reasons former NFL players gave for prescription opioid use during their careers were linked to opioid use and misuse in retirement. Among 336 retired players who had used prescription opioids in the NFL, 26.2% reported use in the past 30 days, including 11.9% who misused them. Using opioids in the NFL to function was associated with any current use, and using them to reduce stress was associated with current misuse.
paper.tldr: Among 336 former NFL players who had used prescription opioids in their careers, using them to function in the NFL was linked to any opioid use after retirement, and stress-relief use was linked to misuse. Sedative and risky alcohol use were common among current users, so screening should cover both.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a telephone survey of retired NFL players conducted in 2010, restricted to the 336 players who had used prescription opioids during their careers (from a parent sample of 644). Players reported reasons for in-career use (to function, change mood, relax or relieve stress, sleep, pain), past-30-day use and misuse, and alcohol and sedative use. Logistic regression tested the reasons as predictors of any current use and of misuse versus use as prescribed, with pain use, alcohol and sedatives included in the models.
paper.findings: Of the 336 players, 14.3% reported use only as prescribed and 11.9% reported misuse in the past 30 days. Use to function in the NFL was reported by 56.8% of current users and 28.2% of non-users (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.50). Among current users, misusers were more likely than those using as prescribed to report stress-relief use in the NFL (35.0% vs 14.6%; OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11) and risky drinking (32.5% vs 12.5%; OR 3.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 10.00). Current users were also far more likely to report sedative use (30.7% vs 4.8%; OR 1.67).
paper.limitations: The sample was restricted to former players who used opioids in the NFL and belong to the players' association, so it may overestimate health and underestimate substance use. The cross-sectional design and self-report data cannot establish cause, and the authors note possible social desirability bias. The findings apply only to professional American football and to 'to function' as a broad category. The Results text gives 35.2% of misusers reporting stress-relief use, while Table 3 gives 35.0%; the table value is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical and team staff could ask players why they use opioids, with particular attention to use to function and to relieve stress, and screen current users for sedative and risky alcohol use. The authors recommend referral to evidence-based pain management for players with chronic pain or misuse.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Opioid use 'to function' during the NFL career was associated with current use in retirement, so staff who prescribe for players should ask why the medication is being taken and record those reasons alongside prescriptions. The study cannot show that changing practice reduces later misuse.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The sample was retired players and the study did not measure return to play after injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or opioid use during rehabilitation. It shows only that in-career reasons for use are associated with later use.
